The Maule tuco-tuco (Ctenomys maulinus) is a fossorial rodent inhabiting the Andean region of central Chile and adjacent Argentina, where it occupies well-drained volcanic soils in high-altitude grasslands. Neonates of this species emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably small body size, with field measurements indicating a wet weight at birth of 12.4 grams [Wwb = 12.4 grams], which represents a minute fraction of the ultimate adult body mass. This altricial state necessitates an extended period of maternal investment within the burrow system before the young can achieve nutritional independence. The suckling stage is characterized by rapid mass gain driven by the high lipid content of the milk, which supports the development of key thermoregulatory and locomotor capabilities. Data from captive colonies suggest that the milk-dependent juvenile phase culminates in weaning, a critical transition that occurs at 36 days after birth [tx = 36 days after birth], after which the offspring begin processing solid plant material independently at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively short dependency period is typical of many subterranean rodents and may be an adaptation to the high energetic costs of lactation for the dam, given the demanding conditions of the hypogean environment.

Under the stable thermal conditions of the burrow, which approximate 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the gestation period of the Maule tuco-tuco has been estimated at 120 days [tg = 120 days], a duration that is considerably longer than that of many other caviomorph rodents of comparable adult body mass. This extended gestation is likely linked to the development of relatively precocial features in the newborn, despite their small mass, and may also reflect the energetic constraints imposed by a low-quality herbivorous diet. Following parturition, the postpartum oestrus permits a rapid return to reproductive cycling. The period of uterine development is followed by lactation and subsequent juvenile growth, with individuals typically attaining the body mass threshold necessary for gonadal activation only after a prolonged post-weaning interval. In these fossorial mammals, the pace of life history transitions is intimately tied to the seasonal availability of high-quality forage, with gestation timed such that parturition coincides with peaks in plant productivity in the austral spring and summer months.

The frequency of these reproductive events is relatively modest, with most females raising approximately 1 litter per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 litter per year], a strategy that reflects the substantial energetic demands of gestation and lactation in a subterranean herbivore. This low annual fecundity is compensated for by the extended longevity of the adults, which allows multiple breeding opportunities across the lifespan. Sexual maturity is not attained until well after the first year; under the constant body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] characteristic of active individuals, puberty occurs at 243 days after birth [tp = 243 days after birth], marking the onset of reproductive viability. This delayed maturation is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth and the acquisition of a stable home burrow system before investing in offspring production.

The mass-specific metabolic rate of these animals supports a slow-paced life history, with sustained investment in tissue maintenance and repair that allows for an extended reproductive window. Field records and captive longevity studies indicate that individuals can survive for a considerable number of years under favorable conditions, as evidenced by a maximum recorded lifespan of 2 years [am = 2 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].

This maximum lifespan of 2 years [am = 2 years], while modest by mammalian standards, is relatively extended for a rodent of its body mass and reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates associated with a protected subterranean existence at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The combination of low reproductive output and delayed puberty places this species firmly within a slow life history continuum, a strategy that is viable largely because of the safety of the burrow environment from most aerial predators.
